question: What is the key difference between Vertical Split and Horizontal Split?

options.text: Vertical Split divides the page by technical layers (header, content, footer)
options.explanation: This describes Horizontal Split. Horizontal division goes by page layers, not by domains.

options.text: Vertical Split means a team owns an entire business domain from UI to API
options.explanation: Exactly: with vertical splitting, Team Catalog owns the catalog pages, components, business logic, and API — the full vertical slice of the product.

options.text: Vertical Split is only used in monorepos
options.explanation: Vertical Split is a decomposition principle not tied to the type of repository. It applies equally to monorepos and polyrepos.

options.text: Vertical Split only suits small teams
options.explanation: The opposite is true: Vertical Split scales especially well with a large number of teams, as it provides maximum autonomy.

question: What is the main role of a Shell application in a micro-frontend architecture?

options.text: To contain all the business logic of the application
options.explanation: The Shell should be as thin as possible. Business logic in the Shell violates team autonomy and creates coupling.

options.text: To act as an orchestrator: load remote MFEs, manage routing, and provide shared context
options.explanation: The Shell is the load-bearing walls of the building: it is responsible for the overall structure, loading parts, global navigation, and shared providers (theme, auth). Business logic is not its job.

options.text: To provide an API for MFEs to communicate with each other
options.explanation: MFEs communicate through events, URLs, or contracts — not through the Shell. The Shell is not a message broker.

options.text: To manage the deployment of all micro-frontend applications
options.explanation: Deployment independence is a key advantage of MFEs. The Shell does not manage the deployment of remote applications.

question: Why is Build-time composition (npm packages) often not considered 'real' MFE?

options.text: Because npm packages cannot be written in React
options.explanation: React components are perfectly fine as npm packages. The problem is not the technology.

options.text: Because deployment independence is lost: updating any MFE requires rebuilding the shell
options.explanation: The main advantage of MFEs is the ability to deploy parts of the application independently. Build-time composition removes this advantage: updating cart-mfe requires rebuilding and redeploying the entire shell.

options.text: Because npm packages do not support TypeScript
options.explanation: npm packages support TypeScript perfectly well and can export types. This is one of their advantages.

options.text: Because npm packages only work with webpack
options.explanation: npm packages work with any bundler. Build-time composition is compatible with Vite, Rollup, esbuild, and others.

question: You are building an e-commerce platform. SEO is critically important. Which type of composition is best suited?

options.text: Client-side composition
options.explanation: CSR is poorly suited for SEO: search bots receive an empty HTML and wait for JavaScript to execute. TTI (Time to Interactive) also increases.

options.text: Server-side composition
options.explanation: Server-side composition delivers ready HTML immediately: search bots see the full content, FCP is minimal. This is the standard choice for public e-commerce pages.

options.text: Build-time composition
options.explanation: Build-time gives good performance metrics but removes deployment independence. For SEO it is sufficient, but edge/server-side gives more flexibility.

options.text: The type of composition does not affect SEO
options.explanation: The type of composition directly affects SEO through FCP and content availability to crawlers. Client-side rendering is a well-known SEO problem.

question: Which dependencies should be made shared (singleton) in Module Federation? Select all correct answers.

options.text: React and ReactDOM
options.explanation: React must be a singleton: different instances break contexts and hooks. This is a mandatory shared dependency.

options.text: React Router
options.explanation: The router creates a global navigation context. Multiple Router instances in one application conflict with each other.

options.text: Utility functions (date-fns, lodash)
options.explanation: Utility libraries do not use global contexts, so they can safely be bundled separately in each MFE. This allows independent versioning.

options.text: HTTP client (axios, ky)
options.explanation: HTTP clients do not require singleton: each MFE can use its own version and configuration. Sharing creates unnecessary coupling.

options.text: Design System with theme
options.explanation: A Design System typically creates a ThemeContext. If each MFE brings its own copy of the DS, contexts will not propagate from the shell to the remote. Singleton is mandatory.

question: A team chose server-side composition and wants to use Redux as shared state. What problem will arise?

options.text: Redux does not support TypeScript
options.explanation: Redux supports TypeScript perfectly and has full type definitions. This is not a problem.

options.text: Hydration problem: the Redux store created on the server will not match the client-side one during hydration
options.explanation: Server-side rendering creates a Redux store with initial state. The client creates its own store. If the states diverge, React will throw a hydration error or re-sync the DOM, causing a visual glitch.

options.text: Redux is too slow for server-side rendering
options.explanation: Redux performance on the server is quite acceptable. The problem is architectural, not performance-related.

options.text: Redux cannot be used with micro-frontends
options.explanation: Redux can be used in MFEs. The problem is specific to combining server-side composition with shared global state, not to MFEs in general.

question: You are using Horizontal Split. The Header team decided to increase the header height from 60px to 80px. What will happen?

options.text: Nothing — the Header MFE is independent and can change its styles
options.explanation: Changing the header size affects the entire page layout. The Content team, Footer team, and everyone else use offsets calculated for 60px.

options.text: All teams must synchronously update their offsets, turning independent deploys into coordinated ones
options.explanation: This is the key drawback of Horizontal Split: changing a layout layer cascades to all other layers. Deployment independence is violated exactly where it was expected.

options.text: The browser automatically adapts the layout
options.explanation: CSS is not aware of the MFE concept. The browser will simply apply the Header MFE styles, which will conflict with the hardcoded offsets of other MFEs.

options.text: The problem is solved through CSS variables in the Design System
options.explanation: CSS variables help if they were used as a contract from the start. But if other MFEs hardcoded their offsets, the variable won't help without updating each MFE.

question: The correct test for defining a micro-frontend boundary is:

options.text: The boundary must align with a React component boundary
options.explanation: React components are too granular a level for MFEs. The infrastructure overhead exceeds the benefit when splitting at this level.

options.text: The boundary must align with an npm package boundary
options.explanation: npm packages are build artifacts, not organizational units. MFE boundaries are defined by business domains, not technical packaging.

options.text: A change within the boundary does not require communication with other teams
options.explanation: This is the main test: if deploying a change requires coordination with another team, the boundary is drawn incorrectly. Team autonomy is the primary criterion.

options.text: The boundary is defined by bundle size (no more than 500 KB)
options.explanation: Bundle size is a performance metric, not a decomposition criterion. An MFE with 50 KB may have a wrong boundary, while an MFE with 2 MB may have a correct one.

question: A team chose Vertical Split with independent deploys and added Redux as a shared singleton. What risk did they create?

options.text: Teams will compete over the structure of the global store
options.explanation: With Vertical Split each team wants isolated logic. A shared Redux store means Team Catalog and Team Cart will conflict when naming slices and reducers.

options.text: With independent deploys, Redux store versions can diverge
options.explanation: If Team Catalog upgraded shared Redux to v5 but Team Cart still uses v4, the singleton will break at runtime. Independent deploys and a shared state manager are poorly compatible.

options.text: Redux is incompatible with TypeScript in an MFE environment
options.explanation: Redux works perfectly with TypeScript in MFEs. The problem is not technical compatibility but architectural coupling.

options.text: Team autonomy is violated: a store change by one team can break another
options.explanation: This is a direct violation of the MFE principle. With Vertical Split, isolated stores or event-driven communication without shared state is preferable.

options.text: A tool for automated micro-frontend deployment
options.explanation: An ADR is a document, not a deployment tool. It records a decision and its context but does not automate any processes.

options.text: A formal document recording an architectural decision with its context, choice, and consequences
options.explanation: An ADR allows future team members to understand not only WHAT was decided but WHY. Context explains the situation, Decision — the choice, Consequences — what is expected.

options.text: A configuration file for Module Federation
options.explanation: Module Federation is configured via webpack.config or vite-plugin-federation. An ADR is an organizational practice for documenting decisions.

options.text: A standard for describing APIs between micro-frontends
options.explanation: APIs between MFEs are described through contracts (TypeScript interfaces, OpenAPI). An ADR records architectural decisions at a higher level.

question: Which inter-MFE communication approach provides the lowest coupling (loose coupling)?

options.text: Direct imports from another MFE
options.explanation: Direct imports create a hard dependency: if the Catalog MFE changes its exports, the Cart MFE will break. This is maximum coupling.

options.text: Shared Redux store as a singleton
options.explanation: Shared state creates implicit coupling through store structure. Changing a slice in one MFE can break another MFE that relies on it.

options.text: Custom Events via window.dispatchEvent
options.explanation: Custom Events follow the publish/subscribe pattern: the producer knows nothing about consumers. MFEs can appear and disappear independently. Loose coupling is achieved through named events.

options.text: Props through the orchestrator (Shell passes data down)
options.explanation: Props through the Shell creates tight coupling: the Shell must know about the data needed by each MFE and becomes the mediator of all communication.
